title: Bulk vs single-cell RNA-seq
objective: Explain what single-cell RNA-seq reveals that bulk RNA-seq hides.

steps.title: Average vs per-cell
steps.body: **[[bulk RNA-seq|Bulk RNA-seq]]** grinds up tissue and reports the *average* expression across all cells. **[[single-cell RNA sequencing|Single-cell RNA-seq]]** measures each cell separately, so you can see distinct cell types and rare populations the average would blur together.

visual.alt: A tissue of mostly-off grey cells with a few bright blue ones. Bulk RNA-seq turns it into one short average bar. Single-cell RNA-seq gives one dot per cell: most dots sit low and a rare subset sits high, and the dashed bulk average falls between the two groups, where no cell actually is.
visual.caption: Bulk gives one blended average; single-cell shows the rare subset that average hides.

steps.prompt: A gene is sky-high in 5% of cells and absent in the rest. What does bulk RNA-seq show?
options: A modest average that hides the real bimodal truth
A clear, sharp picture of just that 5% of cells
Nothing, since 5% is below bulk's detection limit
Each individual cell's value reported separately
steps.explanation: Bulk reports one blended number, so a striking minority pattern looks like a mild average. Single-cell would reveal the two populations.

variants.setup: A gene is very high in a rare subset, off elsewhere.
variants.reveal: Bulk averages over all cells, masking the rare high-expressers.

steps.setup: You want to discover new DRG subtypes defined by marker genes.
steps.reveal: Single-cell RNA-seq is how subtype schemes (like the DRG neuron classes) are discovered — each cell's profile lets you group them into types.

variants.prompt: To find new cell subtypes by expression, use…
variants.explanation: Per-cell profiles are what let you define subtypes.
